blocks.content: Every device on the internet needs an address, exactly like the postal system needs a street address to actually deliver anything, an idea introduced back in the what is a computer network topic. IPv4 and IPv6 are the two addressing schemes in real use today, and understanding why both exist, and why the internet is still in the middle of a slow transition between them, is exactly what this topic covers.

This is not ancient history or a purely academic distinction. Both versions are genuinely in active use right now, on real networks you use every day, and knowing the difference matters for anyone actually building or debugging networked systems.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539703-758750204.png
1. IPv4: The Original, Still Dominant Addressing Scheme
blocks.text: 1. IPv4: The Original, Still Dominant Addressing Scheme

blocks.content: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, written as four numbers separated by dots, like 192.168.1.1, each number ranging from 0 to 255. This format is genuinely easy for a human to read and remember, which is a big part of why it has stuck around so long.

The math behind 32 bits gives exactly 2 to the power of 32 possible addresses, a little over 4.3 billion. That sounded like an enormous, practically unlimited number when IPv4 was designed decades ago, long before phones, smart devices, and billions of new internet connected things existed.
2. The Real Problem: Running Out of Addresses
blocks.text: 2. The Real Problem: Running Out of Addresses

blocks.content: Billions of phones, laptops, servers, and smart devices each need their own address to be reachable on the internet. IPv4 4.3 billion addresses were never actually going to be enough once the internet grew to the scale it has today, and this is not a hypothetical worry, IPv4 address exhaustion is a real, well documented event that has already happened.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539704-904868391.png
blocks.alt: The Real Problem: Running Out of Addresses

blocks.title: A real, dated event, not a future risk
blocks.content: The regional authorities that hand out IPv4 addresses have already run out of fresh blocks to allocate, this genuinely happened, it is not a distant future concern. The internet has been coping with this reality for years already.
3. NAT: A Real but Temporary Workaround
blocks.text: 3. NAT: A Real but Temporary Workaround

blocks.content: Network Address Translation, covered in its own full dedicated topic later in this module, lets many devices behind one router share a single public IPv4 address. This is exactly why your entire home, phones, laptops, smart TV, and everything else, can all reach the internet while your internet provider only actually assigned your router one single public address.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539705-826175208.png
blocks.alt: NAT: A Real but Temporary Workaround

blocks.content: NAT genuinely bought the internet a lot of extra time, but it adds real complexity and does not solve the underlying scarcity, it just hides it behind each router. IPv6 is the actual, permanent fix.
4. IPv6: Room to Grow

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, like 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. That is a genuinely intimidating looking string compared to IPv4 friendly dotted numbers, but the payoff is an address space so enormous it is effectively future proof.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539705-735552255.png
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539705-757424674.png
5. Making IPv6 Addresses More Readable

IPv6 addresses have a real shorthand notation that helps with their length. Consecutive groups of all zeros can be collapsed once, using a double colon, and leading zeros within a group can be dropped entirely. A full address like 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001 compresses down to the much shorter 2001:db8::1.

6. A Simpler, Streamlined Header

Beyond just having more room for addresses, IPv6 also simplified the actual packet header itself compared to IPv4, removing some of the more complex optional fields and streamlining what routers need to process on every single packet. This was a deliberate design choice aimed at faster, more efficient processing at scale.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539706-895905270.png
7. Where We Actually Are Today: A Slow, Ongoing Transition
blocks.text: 7. Where We Actually Are Today: A Slow, Ongoing Transition

blocks.content: Most modern networks and devices actually run both protocols side by side, a setup called dual stack, capable of using whichever one a given connection needs. This transition has been gradual and ongoing for years, not a single overnight switch, and IPv4 still carries a genuinely large share of real internet traffic today, even with IPv6 adoption steadily growing.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785437539707-218532433.png
blocks.alt: Where We Actually Are Today: A Slow, Ongoing Transition

blocks.title: Why the transition is so slow
blocks.content: Every router, every piece of network equipment, and every application across the entire internet would ideally need to support IPv6 for a truly complete switch. Given the internet sheer scale and the fact that NAT keeps IPv4 workable in the meantime, this transition has genuinely taken well over a decade and counting.
8. IPv4 Versus IPv6, Side by Side

9. Common Mistakes and Key Takeaways

["Assuming IPv6 has fully replaced IPv4 already, when both are genuinely in active, simultaneous use today, running side by side as dual stack.","Assuming NAT is a permanent fix for address scarcity, when it is a real but temporary workaround, IPv6 is the actual long term solution.","IPv4 uses 32 bit addresses, about 4.3 billion total, and is running out.","IPv6 uses 128 bit addresses, an effectively future proof amount of space.","NAT lets many devices share one public IPv4 address, buying time but adding complexity.","The transition to IPv6 has been gradual, most networks run both protocols side by side today."]
items: Assuming IPv6 has fully replaced IPv4 already, when both are genuinely in active, simultaneous use today, running side by side as dual stack.
Assuming NAT is a permanent fix for address scarcity, when it is a real but temporary workaround, IPv6 is the actual long term solution.
IPv4 uses 32 bit addresses, about 4.3 billion total, and is running out.
IPv6 uses 128 bit addresses, an effectively future proof amount of space.
NAT lets many devices share one public IPv4 address, buying time but adding complexity.
The transition to IPv6 has been gradual, most networks run both protocols side by side today.
